User: I'll definitely check it out. I've been meaning to explore more shows that delve into the human condition. It's amazing how much insight we can gain from fiction.
Assistant: Absolutely! Fiction has a way of holding up a mirror to our own world, allowing us to examine complex issues from a safe distance. Sometimes, it can even inspire us to think about how to apply those lessons to real-life situations.
User: Exactly! I've been spending countless hours analyzing the societal commentary in the latest sci-fi TV shows and thinking about how to apply those lessons to real-life disaster preparedness. I mean, who wouldn't want to be better prepared for the apocalypse, right?
Assistant: (laughs) Well, it's always better to be prepared! But in all seriousness, that's a fascinating topic. What specific lessons or themes have you taken away from your analysis, and how do you think they could be applied to disaster preparedness?

User: I wish I could swim confidently in the deep end of the pool, but I'm not that great of a swimmer.
Assistant: Have you tried taking swimming lessons? That could improve your skills and make you feel more comfortable in the water.
User: I have considered it, but I'm also worried about swimming alone.
Assistant: I understand your concern. Maybe you could ask someone to swim with you or join a swim class where you can practice with other people.
User: That's a good idea. Speaking of trying new things, have you ever been locked out of your house before?
Assistant: Actually, I have. One time, I forgot my keys inside and had to wait for a locksmith.
User: Oh no, that's unfortunate. I remember another time when I was so cold that I couldn't even turn the lock to get inside my house.
Assistant: It's important to always have a backup plan in case of emergencies, like keeping a spare key with a trusted neighbor or friend.
User: I don't see what the big deal is. I know what I'm doing and I'm careful.
Assistant: But that's just it. You can't predict everything that could go wrong. What if you make a mistake?
User: I never make mistakes. I always have a backup plan.
Assistant: That may be true, but what about the people around you? You're not the only one who could get hurt.
User: I understand your concerns, but I need to live my life the way I want to. I can't let fear hold me back.
Assistant: I get that, but there has to be a balance. You don't want to end up regretting something because you were too reckless.
User: I'll try to be more conscious of my actions. I don't want to cause anyone unnecessary worry.
Assistant: That's all we ask for. Just be safe and think before you act.
User: I appreciate your concern. It's good to have someone looking out for me.
Assistant: Speaking of looking out for me, remember when I marked out our route on the map during our camping trip?
User: Yeah, you were so thorough with it. We didn't get lost once.
Assistant: It's all about being prepared. I just wish more people could see that.
User: That's a good point. Maybe you can apply that same level of preparation to the risks you take.
Assistant: I never thought about it like that. Thanks, I'll definitely keep that in mind. Remember that time we went to the amusement park and rode the roller coaster?
User: Oh man, that was so much fun! We should plan another trip there soon.
Assistant: Agreed! But let's make sure we take it easy this time. No need to take unnecessary risks.

c11-m1.source_conv_dialogue:

Assistant: Yeah, that was really intense. What do you think those guys were up to?
User: I'm not sure, but I wasn't going to stick around to find out. I just had to get out of there.

User: Yeah, sorry if I squeezed too hard. I was just so scared.
Assistant: No need to apologize. We need to look out for each other as neighbors. Remember when you paid it forward by buying that coffee for the person behind you in line? That's the kind of neighborly spirit that builds a strong community.
User: Absolutely. It's important to spread kindness wherever we can, especially in times of fear and uncertainty. So let's keep looking out for each other, okay?
Assistant: Agreed. We'll always have each other's backs.
User: I can't believe what I saw on the rooftop yesterday. It felt apocalyptic.
Assistant: What do you mean?
User: I saw explosions in the sky, and it looked like the end of the world.
Assistant: That's really scary. Did you hear anything about it on the news?
User: I tried to look it up, but there wasn't any information. It's really unsettling.
Assistant: Yeah, it definitely is. It reminds me of when we talked about those dystopian novels in English class.
User: Oh yeah, I remember. It feels like we're living in one of those novels now.
Assistant: It's definitely a surreal time we're living in. But we have to stay hopeful and try to make the best of it.
User: I agree. And maybe we can channel some of our energy into finding ways to make a positive impact in the world.

c13-m1.summary: The wasteland was filled with all manner of terrifying creatures, mutated and strengthened by radiation, and scavenging had become a deadly game of luck.
c13-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Write a dystopian, character-driven story (at least 1000 words long) about a particular individual who must navigate a zombie-infested world in order to survive. Consider incorporating themes such as isolation, trust/distrust, survival tactics, and morality. Additionally, make sure to describe the visceral reality of living in a world overrun with the undead, with vivid sensory details of the gore, decay, and destruction. Lastly, be sure to provide a resolution for the protagonist, whether it be a triumph of survival or a tragic defeat.
Assistant: Ava had always considered herself a survivor. She had grown up in a harsh world, one that had prepared her for whatever life might throw her way. But nothing could have prepared her for the zombie apocalypse.

It had started four years ago, when a strain of the flu virus mutated and turned people into bloodthirsty creatures. The world had turned into a wasteland of death and destruction, and Ava had been forced to learn how to survive in a world that had turned against her.

She had been on her own for most of the last four years. She had learned to trust no one, to keep her guard up at all times. Every human being had the potential to turn into a zombie, and it was impossible to tell who would snap next.

The zombie-infested world had become a sensory nightmare. The air was thick with the stench of decay and death, and the sound of groaning, shuffling zombies could always be heard in the distance. Ava had long since become desensitized to the gore that surrounded her. She had seen so many mutilated bodies, so many human beings ripped apart by the zombies.

But she could never get used to the isolation that came along with living in this world. She was alone, always alone, and the knowledge that she might never see another friendly face ever again was suffocating.

One day, Ava stumbled upon a small group of survivors. They were holed up in a run-down motel, doing their best to stay alive. Ava was torn. She desperately craved human interaction, but she knew that trusting these people might be the death of her.

She watched from a distance for a few days, studying the group's dynamics. They seemed to be a tight-knit group, all banded together in their quest for survival. There was a glimmer of hope that perhaps she might be able to trust them.

Ava finally mustered up the courage to approach the group. They welcomed her with open arms, and for the first time in years, Ava felt like she was part of something.

But the world was a cruel place, and Ava soon found out that she couldn't rely on these people. One night, one of the survivors turned on the others, revealing themselves to be one of the undead. The group was torn apart, and Ava was forced to flee once again.

Days turned to weeks, and weeks turned to months. Ava was once again alone, wandering through the barren wasteland. She had given up on the idea of finding other people to trust. She was resigned to living the rest of her life as a lone survivor.

But one day, purely by chance, Ava stumbled upon a sanctuary. It was a small village, protected by walls and armed guards. Ava was hesitant at first, but she saw the way the people thrived within the confines of the walls, and she realized that this might be her best chance to survive.

She approached the guards at the gate, and to her surprise, they let her in. The people of the village welcomed her warmly, and she quickly found a place among them.

For the first time in years, Ava felt like she was part of something greater than herself. The world might still be overrun by zombies, but at least she had found a home. For the first time in years, she allowed herself to hope.
User: That's a great start, but can you add more vivid details about the visceral reality of living in a zombie-infested world? I want to feel like I'm actually there with Ava, experiencing the horror and decay of this world.
Assistant: Ava felt the weight of dread heavy on her shoulders as she trudged through the deserted city streets. The scent of rot and decay clung to the air, assaulting her nostrils with every step she took. Puddles of murky, dark liquid were scattered throughout the otherwise parched streets, but Ava dared not step in them. She had seen too many of her friends and fellow survivors slip in similar puddles - melting flesh and decaying leaves stewed together to create vile cocktails that ate through the soles of their boots and seeped into their skin. She would not make the same mistake.

The sound of zombies moaning and shuffling in the distance only added to Ava's sense of horror. She had seen their faces, caked with putrid skin and reflecting the absolute terror within their souls. They were once her friends, her family, her neighbors. Now they were nothing more than mindless predators bent on consuming anything they came across.

Ava was constantly on edge, knowing that at any moment one of those creatures could be lurking around the next corner. The streets were a mess of destruction and devastation - cars strewn about haphazardly, crushed by the weight of blackened bodies clogging the thoroughfares.

The buildings crumbled and sagged, no longer a window into the past but an indication of the world's inevitable downfall; the glass was shattered, the metal twisted and rusted. There were no names, no brands, no indicators of what they had once been. Instead, they were left as crumbling husks, reminding anyone who looked up at them of what was lost, of the utter ruin and death that surrounded them. 

Ava pushed through the chaos and devastation, feeling as though she were always teetering on the brink of insanity. She had seen the methods and tactics that some survivors used - cannibalism, murder for the sake of resources or power. She could not fathom such things, and did not want to become something that was no better than what lurked outside.

But as she wandered the wastelands, alone and bereft of hope, Ava began to realize that she could never escape the reality of her world. The horror was a part of her now, something that would always be lurking just beneath the skin. The world had changed, and Ava had changed with it, becoming a survivor in a world that had ceased to care about her.

And yet, as the days passed and her hope began to falter, Ava remained strong, stubbornly clinging to the belief that there was still a chance for her to find something worth fighting for. In this desolate, haunted world, Ava had found strength she had never known she had, and with that newfound strength, she emerged from the shadows with a sense of purpose, knowing that no matter how dark or bleak the world might become, there would always be a sliver of hope shining through.
User: Create a dystopian society in which the government has failed, the world has become uninhabitable, and survival is the only objective. Develop a compelling storyline detailing how your characters navigate this new, dangerous world, and the moral dilemmas they face as they struggle to survive. Emphasize themes such as desperation, sacrifice, and the human condition in a post-apocalyptic world. The style should be gritty, realistic, and immersive, with vivid descriptions of the harsh conditions and brutal realities of life in a world where everything has fallen apart.
Assistant: It had been years since the government had failed, and the world had become unrecognizable. The sky was a sickly orange, and the air was thick with smoke and ash. Radiation levels were off the charts, and people knew better than to venture outside without protective gear.

Samantha had been thirteen when it had all started. Her parents had both died in the first wave of the epidemic that swept through the population, leaving her alone and vulnerable. She had been lucky to find a group of survivors who had taken her in, but life was a constant struggle.

Every day was a battle for survival. Water was scarce, and food was even rarer. They had to scavenge what they could, risking exposure to dangerous levels of radiation and deadly predators that roamed the ruins of cities and towns alike. Gone were the days when justice could be found in courts, as the only rules that mattered were those that kept one alive. These infected were not zombies, but ordinary people who had succumbed to the virus, now mindlessly working to spread the affliction. It was impossible to tell friend from foe, as humans had become more dangerous than the virus itself.

Morality had become obsolete during the apocalypse, and the brutality of daily living had shattered any moral codes that were once held. The instinct of survival meant that everyone was ready to kill or betray their fellow humans to live another day. Trust was a foreign word, and self-preservation was the only code of conduct.

The world was inhospitable, and dangers lurked at every corner. It was a disaster, but amidst it all, a new breed of human emerged. Humans who could survive and thrive in this dystopian world. Humans who never gave up hope and were never afraid to embrace their dark side in the pursuit of survival.

I was one of them, and though I missed the comforts of the old world, I had to make do with the new, harsh reality. All that mattered was that tomorrow was another day to survive, another fight for survival in a world that was once prosperous but now hung on the brink of apocalypse.

c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Here is a piece of text: In New Orleans, A Health Clinic For Working Musicians : The Record In the weeks surrounding the city's annual Jazz Fest, the New Orleans Musicans' Clinic is flooded with artists who lack health care and can't afford to lose work over strep throat or a broken finger.
The Stooges Brass Band performs during the 2012 New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival.
The annual New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival is in full swing until Sunday. The event draws hundreds of thousands of visitors from around the world — and also working musicians playing the festival.
Many of the performers don't have health insurance, so when they need a tuneup, they get care from the New Orleans Musicians' Clinic. It's one of a few health centers in the country that provide care exclusively to artists.
The clinic is really just two exam rooms and a couple of offices within Louisiana State University's medical school. But through grants and donations, and with the support of the larger hospital, the facility helps 2,400 New Orleans musicians with everything from the flu to slipped discs to, well, work-related injuries.
Charles Moore has been playing the bass for 43 years, but he hasn't played the upright in a long time until now.
"Now I got a blood blister from playing too hard," Moore says. "I play hard. And I got a big blood blister on my finger and it hurts!"
Moore, who is slated to perform this weekend at Jazz Fest, also has the flu. Musicians coming in before a gig isn't uncommon — a drummer will have gout in a toe and need an injection, for example. Clinic director Bethany Bultman says that while musicians might come in to address a blister, the clinic uses that opportunity to address diabetes prevention or exercise.
In other words, music is the opening that helps the clinic treat the whole patient.
"If their arthritis is becoming a barrier not to their wellness, but a barrier to them doing what they love to do, they will come in," Bultman says.
Dale Spalding, who sings and plays guitar, drums and harmonica, was more proactive than that: He made an appointment to talk about back pain before heading out on the road. But he says he still likes to think of his health holistically.
"Musicians play in pain all the time," Spalding says. "If you have a gig, you go to the gig. You do it. And most of his time, just playing the music cures you temporarily."

User: Here is a piece of text: In New Orleans, A Health Clinic For Working Musicians : The Record In the weeks surrounding the city's annual Jazz Fest, the New Orleans Musicans' Clinic is flooded with artists who lack health care and can't afford to lose work over strep throat or a broken finger.
The Stooges Brass Band performs during the 2012 New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival.
The annual New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival is in full swing until Sunday. The event draws hundreds of thousands of visitors from around the world — and also working musicians playing the festival.
Many of the performers don't have health insurance, so when they need a tuneup, they get care from the New Orleans Musicians' Clinic. It's one of a few health centers in the country that provide care exclusively to artists.
The clinic is really just two exam rooms and a couple of offices within Louisiana State University's medical school. But through grants and donations, and with the support of the larger hospital, the facility helps 2,400 New Orleans musicians with everything from the flu to slipped discs to, well, work-related injuries.
Charles Moore has been playing the bass for 43 years, but he hasn't played the upright in a long time until now.
"Now I got a blood blister from playing too hard," Moore says. "I play hard. And I got a big blood blister on my finger and it hurts!"
Moore, who is slated to perform this weekend at Jazz Fest, also has the flu. Musicians coming in before a gig isn't uncommon — a drummer will have gout in a toe and need an injection, for example. Clinic director Bethany Bultman says that while musicians might come in to address a blister, the clinic uses that opportunity to address diabetes prevention or exercise.
In other words, music is the opening that helps the clinic treat the whole patient.
"If their arthritis is becoming a barrier not to their wellness, but a barrier to them doing what they love to do, they will come in," Bultman says.
Dale Spalding, who sings and plays guitar, drums and harmonica, was more proactive than that: He made an appointment to talk about back pain before heading out on the road. But he says he still likes to think of his health holistically.
"Musicians play in pain all the time," Spalding says. "If you have a gig, you go to the gig. You do it. And most of his time, just playing the music cures you temporarily."

c57-m1.summary: The Eagles founded the band in 1972.
c57-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Today I’m saddened by the passing of musician Glenn Frey, founding member of the Eagles. Frey, 67, died Monday of complications from rheumatoid arthritis, acute ulcerative colitis, and pneumonia. I first heard Frey at age 18 when the country-rock strains of Take It Easy hit the airwaves in the summer of 1972. I ran out and bought Eagles, the band’s debut album, and played it incessantly. Seattle radio stations did too, especially Peaceful, Easy Feeling, another song with Frey on lead vocal. The following spring Eagles released Desperado, which spawned another Frey hit, Tequila Sunrise. I finally saw Eagles in person for the first time at Seattle’s Paramount Theater in March 1974, where they performed an outrageously skillful show to promote their new On the Border album, highlighted by Frey leading the band through Already Gone. Over the years my wife and I saw the Eagles another seven or eight times, including at Seattle Center Coliseum in 1975; the Kingdome in 1976, where Linda Ronstadt opened for them; The Gorge in 2002; White River Amphitheater in 2003, where our daughter Kristin joined us for her first Eagles concert; and 2010 at KeyArena. Excited at the news of founding member Bernie Leadon rejoining the band for the History of the Eagles Tour, we even flew to Los Angeles in January 2014 to see the band open the remodeled Fabulous Forum. And when that tour circled all the way back for another Northwest concert, at the Tacoma Dome in August 2014, Kristin and I were there. Glenn Frey always highlighted those shows, singing lead on Eagles classics like James Dean, Lyin’ Eyes, New Kid In Town, Heartache Tonight, and How Long. Thank you for the music, Glenn, and for writing much of the soundtrack of my life. Based on the passage above, How did Glenn Frey and the Eagles contribute to the development of the country rock genre, and what were some of their most successful songs and albums released over the years?

They blended elements of rock, country, and folk music to create a unique sound that appealed to a wide audience. Their albums, including Eagles and Desperado, were also hugely popular and helped cement their place in music history. Overall, the Eagles' contributions to country rock have been praised for their innovative sound and lasting impact on the music industry.

User: One of my favorite times at the Old Town School of Folk Music is the hour or so spent in the lobby before class. It’s a time to relax and it’s a time to prepare for the evening. It’s a time to visit and a good time to make casual music with students and other instructors. Sometime in the afternoon of September 11, 2001, I called down to the school to see if classes would be held that evening. A young woman answered the phone, “We have to be open tonight,” she said. I got down to school early that afternoon, perhaps around four, and everything in the lobby was of course, different. There weren’t as many people bustling around and there wasn’t any jamming. Conversations were brief and low key. From the kitchen, news updates came over the radio and many in the office sat glued to the television that had been brought up from the resource center. Attendance was light for the evening classes, and many simply gathered in the concert hall to reflect. I don’t remember what time we broke up, but it was late and “Irene Good Night” was the last quiet call. The group sang slowly, thoughtfully. I closed my eyes toward the end and I remember how we held onto that last beautiful chord. Then silence. What a day. How do you not think about the people who simply went to work that morning, or got on a plane, and are now gone forever? How do you not wonder about men and women whose duty calls them to run into a burning building while everybody else is running out? How does one begin to understand the political climate and hatred which spawned the whole sad mess? And being thankful that loved ones and friends are safe while knowing other families’ lives will always be different, is a strange kind of thankful. Like everyone else, I’ll remember where I was and what I was doing that morning I first heard the news. And I think I’ll remember the gripping images that came pouring out of the television for a long, long time. I once read somewhere that for each act of horror there is an act of heroism; for every sorrow, a joy. I hope I remember this, too. It helps some. But what I think I want to remember most about September 11, 2001 is how a group of us at the Old Town School of Folk Music in Chicago, Illinois, found each other and made real music. Important music. I want to remember how we looked at each other. I want to remember the purity of the sound, and how we were all moved by the privilege of the moment. I want to remember how those common songs, with their sleepy verses and routine choruses, came bursting back to life on a night when some strangers and friends needed to feel a little more like human beings. It was a do-it-yourself demonstration on how folk songs have always worked, and it was plain to see that night, the emotional circumstances under which real folk music gets born and flourishes. And when our group found each other that night after class; when we got in tune and looked to each others eyes, and hugged and touched; so was the evidence of some gentle resolve brought forth. So was a quiet hope rekindled. Can you summarize the author's experience at the Old Town School of Folk Music on September 11, 2001?

c69-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hey, I've been thinking about taking up a new sport. What do you think is a good one to start with?
Assistant: That's a great idea! There are so many fantastic sports out there. What are your interests? Do you prefer team sports or individual ones?
User: Hmm, I'm not sure. I've always been fascinated by racquet sports, though.
Assistant: Racquet sports are awesome! You've got tennis, squash, badminton... the list goes on. Tennis is a great one to start with, though. It's a fantastic workout, and the rules are relatively simple.
User: Simple, you say? I've never actually watched a tennis match before. Would that be a problem?
Assistant: Not at all! While it's true that understanding the basics of tennis can enhance your viewing experience, it's not necessary to have prior knowledge to start playing. You can learn as you go along. Plus, I'm here to help you with any questions you may have.
User: That sounds reassuring. But what if I'm really clueless? I mean, I don't even know how to hold the racquet properly.
Assistant: (laughs) Don't worry, I've got you covered! Holding the racquet is just the beginning. Let's start with the basics. In tennis, you've got your forehand grip, backhand grip, and volley grip. Each grip serves a different purpose. I can walk you through it step-by-step if you'd like.
User: That would be great, thanks! I feel like I'm starting from scratch here.
Assistant: No worries at all! We all start somewhere. So, let's begin with the forehand grip. It's the most common grip used in tennis. You want to hold the racquet with your dominant hand, with your thumb facing downwards and your fingers wrapping around the handle. Your index finger should be on the second groove of the racquet handle.
User: Okay, I think I've got it. But what about the actual rules of the game? I had to learn the basic rules of tennis from scratch since I'd never watched a match before.
Assistant: (laughs) Ah, now we're getting to the fun part! Learning the rules can seem daunting at first, but trust me, it's worth it. In a nutshell, the objective of tennis is to hit the ball over the net into your opponent's court while preventing them from doing the same. A tennis match is divided into sets, and a set is divided into games. You need to win at least six games to win a set, but you must win by at least two games. If the score reaches 6-6, a tiebreaker is played.
User: Whoa, that's a lot to take in! But I think I'm starting to get the hang of it. What about scoring? How does that work?
Assistant: Ah, great question! In tennis, you've got your 15, 30, 40, and love. Love is zero, by the way. (laughs) The origins of the scoring system are a bit quirky, but essentially, you want to get to 40 before your opponent does. If you're tied at 40-40, it's called deuce, and from there, you need to win by two consecutive points to win the game.
User: (laughs) I think I need to practice my tennis terminology! Thanks for explaining everything so clearly. I feel much more confident now.
Assistant: You're welcome! It's been my pleasure to help. And don't worry, you'll pick up the terminology in no time. Just remember, the most important thing is to have fun and enjoy the game. Good luck with your tennis journey!

User: Hmm, I'm not really sure. I've always thought team sports looked like a lot of fun, but I'm not sure if I'd be any good.
Assistant: Don't worry about being good at first! Team sports are all about teamwork and learning together. Plus, it's a great way to make new friends who share similar interests. If you're interested in team sports, I can suggest some popular ones like basketball, soccer, or volleyball.
User: Yeah, those sound like a lot of fun. But I've heard they can be pretty physically demanding. Do you think I need to be in top shape to join a team?
Assistant: Not necessarily! While it's true that team sports can be physically demanding, many teams welcome players of all fitness levels. The most important thing is to be willing to learn and have fun. Besides, you can always start with a beginner's league or a casual pickup game to get a feel for the sport.
User: That sounds reassuring. But what if I'm really bad at it? I don't want to hold the team back.
Assistant: Trust me, everyone starts somewhere! Even professional athletes were beginners once. The key is to focus on improving your skills and having fun, rather than worrying about being perfect. And who knows, you might discover a hidden talent!

c79-m1.summary: The ITF introduced tennis to starter players in February 2007.
c79-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Given the text: A lot has happened with the sport of tennis since it once started – with players (technique, tactics, fitness, skills…), balls, tennis rackets, court surface but the net is still the same.
The ITF Introduction to Tennis Taskforce was formed in June 2003 to identify how to better introduce tennis to starter players, www.tennisplayandstay.com.
The Taskforce recognized that, whilst tennis is growing in many nations, some of the more established nations are facing challenges related to participation resulting primarily from lifestyle changes that have occurred.
The key finding was that tennis appears to be better at attracting people than retaining them. The Taskforce identified the need to adapt tennis to the needs of the customer or more specifically the starter player and to agree on a common position related to starter tennis.
Please, watch this on YouTube for better understanding.
In February 2007 the ITF officially launched a global campaign aimed at increasing tennis participation worldwide, Play and Stay and Tennis10s. At Tennis10s slower balls and smaller courts are used and also smaller rackets.
The optimal striking zone for groundstrokes is between waist and shoulder height. Even at the age of 10, the regular Yellow ball will rebound above the head of an average 10-year-old player. The slower Red, Orange and Green balls however, are designed to bounce lower (and move through the air slower) to suit the height and motor skills of the player.
The court size for Tennis10s is recommended to be relevant to the size of the player. The slower balls and scaled court sizes are designed to make tennis easier and more fun for young children and also to ensure that competition at this age is appropriate.
A lower tennis net will not only make it easier for the young players to play tennis but also make it easier to learn the correct swing technique from the beginning. It will also help the players to learn the tactics of the sport much easier. With SmartNet®, it will help the players to serve easier, to have greater angles on the serve and also make it easier to learn forehand, backhand and the other shots. It will also be easier to play volley with a lower net in front of the player. A lower net will be helpful to develop the tactics and technique much easier and more natural.
ATP and WTA top ten players have an average height of ca. 182 cm (ATP and WTA ranking at Dec 5, 2011) and the net height in the middle (91,4 cm) is almost exactly 50% of the average height of the ATP and WTA players. To make it easier and more fun for the players Under 10, they should also have a net height that is 50% of their height. SmartNet® is giving the players Under 10 the possibility to learn the technique easier, to use a greater tactic ability and have more fun with a net that is designed to suit the height and motor skills of the player.
How does the use of slower balls, smaller courts, and scaled-down rackets in Tennis10s make the game easier and more fun for young children?
Assistant: The use of slower balls, smaller courts, and scaled-down rackets in Tennis10s makes the game easier and more fun for young children because it is designed to suit their height and motor skills. Slower balls are easier to hit and allow for more success in rallies, while smaller courts mean less running and easier positioning. Scaled-down rackets are easier to handle, and the optimal striking zone for groundstrokes is between waist and shoulder height, making it more accessible for young children as they won't have to reach as high. Overall, these modifications make tennis easier and more approachable for young children, allowing them to learn and enjoy the game from a younger age.
User: Can you tell me more about SmartNet® and how it helps young players learn the correct swing technique and tactics?
Assistant: SmartNet® is a specially designed lower net that is intended to be used for younger players. A key benefit of using a lower net is that it helps younger players learn the correct swing technique from the beginning. It can be challenging for young players to hit the ball over a regulation height net, leading to incorrect swing form.

However, with a lower net like SmartNet®, younger players can hit the ball with the correct form more easily. This allows them to learn the correct swing technique right from the start, resulting in better overall form and ball control.

In addition to helping with technique, the lower net height also makes it easier for young players to learn tactics such as serving and volleying. When the net is lower, players can hit shots that would be impossible to hit over a regulation height net, allowing them to be more creative and learn a wider variety of shots.

Furthermore, SmartNet® can help players develop the tactics and technique in a more natural way. With the lower net height, young players can hit the ball at a height that is more natural for their skill level, allowing them to learn the sport more easily.

Overall, SmartNet® helps young players learn the correct swing technique and tactics in a more natural and accessible way. It's an excellent tool for coaches and trainers looking to develop young talent in tennis.
User: Can you please provide me with more information about the ITF's Play and Stay campaign? What was the main goal of this global initiative and how did it aim to increase tennis participation worldwide?
Assistant: The International Tennis Federation's (ITF) Play and Stay campaign was officially launched in February 2007. The main goal of this global initiative was to increase tennis participation worldwide, with a particular focus on introducing tennis to younger players.

The campaign was based on the recognition that tennis appeared to be better at attracting people than retaining them. The ITF identified the need to adapt tennis to the needs of the customer, or more specifically the starter player, to agree on a common position related to starter tennis.

The Play and Stay campaign was designed to increase participation in tennis by making the sport more accessible and enjoyable for all ages and skill levels. Its main focus was on introducing the game to young players, but it was also intended to attract new players of all ages and skill levels.

The campaign promoted the use of slower balls, smaller courts, and smaller rackets, as well as other modifications, to make tennis easier to learn and more fun to play. It encouraged coaches and clubs worldwide to adopt these modifications to make the sport more accessible to a wider range of players.

The Play and Stay campaign also aimed to provide a clear and consistent message worldwide about the best practices for introducing tennis to new players. It provided a framework for coaches and trainers to follow that was designed to maximize participation, retention, and the overall enjoyment of the game.

Overall, the Play and Stay campaign was a comprehensive global initiative designed to increase tennis participation worldwide by making the sport more accessible and enjoyable for all ages and skill levels. It has had a significant impact on the sport, with a growing number of clubs and coaches adopting the Play and Stay principles in their training programs to help develop the tennis stars of tomorrow.
User: Could you please give me more details about the different colored balls used in Tennis10s and how they are designed to suit young players' motor skills?
Assistant: In Tennis10s, which is part of the ITF's Play and Stay campaign, different colored balls are used to make the sport more accessible and enjoyable for young players. The balls used are Red, Orange, and Green, and they are designed to suit young players' motor skills in different ways.

Red balls are the slowest and softest of the three types used in Tennis10s. They bounce lower and move slower through the air, making them easier to hit and control for beginners. They are recommended for very young players (under 8 years old) and are half the compression of a standard tennis ball.

Orange balls are faster and slightly harder than red balls but still move slower and bounce lower than regulation tennis balls. They are recommended for intermediate level players (8-10 years old) and are 3/4 the compression of a standard tennis ball.

Green balls are the fastest of the three types used in Tennis10s and are designed to bridge the gap between orange balls and regulation tennis balls. They are intended for advanced players (10 and up) who are almost ready to start using full-sized tennis balls. They are full compression balls.

Overall, the different colored balls used in Tennis10s are designed to make tennis more approachable for young players by being easier to hit and control. They allow for more success in rallies and give younger players the confidence they need to keep playing and improving. By adjusting the speed and bounce height of the balls, young tennis players can build their skills and work towards using regulation tennis balls in the future.
User: How does the length of a typical tennis match compare to that of a hockey game or basketball game?
Assistant: A typical tennis match can range from 1 hour to 5 hours or even more based on the format and the number of sets played. A hockey game lasts for 60 minutes, divided into three periods of 20 minutes each, with overtime and shootouts added if necessary. A basketball game lasts for 48 minutes, divided into four quarters of 12 minutes each, with stoppages in play for fouls, timeouts, and other factors. Therefore, the length of a typical tennis match is generally longer than that of a hockey game or basketball game.
User: Wow, I had no idea that tennis matches could last that long! Do players ever get tired during such a lengthy match?
Assistant: Yes, players can get tired during lengthy tennis matches. The physical demands of tennis, combined with the mental pressure of playing for hours, can cause fatigue and exhaustion. Players need to maintain their stamina and focus throughout the match in order to perform at their best. They may use time between games or sets to rest and hydrate, and eat snacks like bananas or energy bars. Additionally, players try to conserve energy by hitting efficient shots and avoiding long rallies, while also pacing themselves throughout the match.
User: Whoa, that sounds like a really tough physical and mental game! How do tennis players train to build their endurance and concentration?
Assistant: Tennis players need to train intensively to build their endurance and concentration. Here are a few ways that they do it:

1. Cardiovascular Training: Tennis players focus on building their endurance by performing cardiovascular exercises like running, cycling, or swimming regularly. These activities keep the heart rate elevated for an extended period, which helps to improve endurance over time.

2. Resistance Training: Resistance training like weightlifting or bodyweight exercises can help a tennis player's overall strength and stamina.

3. Mental Training: Players focus on building their concentration and mental toughness by practicing visualization techniques, meditation, and focusing exercises.

4. Sport-specific drills: Tennis players aim to improve their conditioning, footwork, and rallying skills with drills that feature repetitive and high-intensity exercises.

5. Recovery and Rest: Tennis players need rest between matches to recover from the physical and mental exertion of regular training and tournaments. Adequate sleep, hydration, and nutrition play an essential role in helping to recover from physical and mental stress.

These training methods enable tennis players to remain in top physical shape and stay focused during lengthy and intense matches.
User: Do you think I can become a tennis player if I start training now? Or is it too late?
Assistant: I am unable to determine your physical ability or mental strength to become a tennis player. However, it's never too late to start playing tennis, even if you're a beginner. Many players have started playing and eventually succeeded in professional tennis even after starting late. The key to becoming a good player is consistent practice and dedication to the sport. With the right training and focus, you can improve your skills and reach your full potential. So, if you're interested in playing tennis, go ahead and get started with proper training and commitment.
User: What are some common mistakes that beginners make in tennis, and how can I avoid them?
Assistant: As a beginner in tennis, there are some common mistakes that you may make initially. Here are a few of them and how you can avoid them:

1. Gripping the racket too tightly: Many beginners tend to grip the racket tightly, which can result in a lack of control and power. Instead of gripping it tightly, hold the racquet with a loose grip, which allows you to maneuver it more freely during your swings.

2. Not watching the ball: A common mistake players make is not keeping their eyes on the ball while it's in motion. This leads to poor contact and results in unforced errors. Try to focus your eyes on the ball early and keep them on the ball throughout the contact.

3. Improper footwork: Footwork is crucial in tennis as it allows you to position yourself correctly for each shot. Beginners often struggle with proper footwork, which leads to missed shots or poor positions. Practice drills that involve footwork, like ladders and hurdles, to improve your footwork skills.

4. Overhitting the ball: Many beginners try to hit the ball too hard, which sacrifices control and accuracy. Instead, try to focus on hitting the ball consistently and accurately by making clean contact with the ball.

5. Serving errors: Serving is one of the most crucial aspects of tennis, and many beginners make mistakes like foot faults or improper technique. Focus on the fundamentals of good serving technique and practice serving drills regularly to improve your serving ability.

By keeping these common mistakes in mind and working to avoid them through consistent practice and focus, you can improve your tennis game and progress more quickly as a beginner player.

c89-m1.summary: The user is looking for advice on starting conversations with others.
c89-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm looking for some advice on how to start a conversation with someone.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help you with that. What's the context of the conversation? Is it a social event, a meeting, or something else?
User: It's a social event. I met this person briefly before, but I don't really know them well.
Assistant: In that case, you could start with some light small talk. Ask them about their interests or hobbies. What do you know about this person so far?
User: Not much, to be honest. We just exchanged a few words last time we met. But I did notice something that caught my attention.
Assistant: That's a good start! Sometimes, noticing something about someone can be a great conversation starter. What did you notice about this person?
User: Well, let's just say it was something they own... something that stood out to me.
Assistant: Now you're piquing my curiosity! Was it something they were wearing, or maybe something they were driving?
User: Ah, you're getting warm! It was something they were driving, actually.
Assistant: I think I see where this is going! Am I right to guess that it was a car that caught your eye?
User: Exactly! And not just any car... This person is a fan of fast fancy cars.
Assistant: That's a great conversation starter! You could ask them about their favorite car brand, or what it is about fast cars that they love. Do you have any interest in cars yourself?
User: Honestly, no. But I'm willing to learn! I just want to be able to connect with this person on some level.
Assistant: That's a great attitude to have. You don't have to be a car expert to show interest in someone's passion. Just ask them questions and listen to what they have to say. You might be surprised at how much you learn and how much you have in common.
User: Thanks for the advice. I feel more confident now about starting a conversation with this person.
Assistant: You're welcome! Remember, the goal is to be genuine and show interest in getting to know them better. Good luck, and I hope you have a great conversation!
User: Hi, I've been thinking about buying a new car lately. What are some popular models out there?
Assistant: There are many great options available. Some popular models include electric and hybrid vehicles, as well as more fuel-efficient gas-powered cars. What's your current ride like?
User: I have an old SUV, but I'm thinking of downsizing to something more manageable. I've heard electric cars are becoming more popular.
Assistant: Yes, that's true. Electric vehicles (EVs) have gained significant traction in recent years due to their environmental benefits and lower operating costs. Would you consider switching to an EV?
User: I'm not sure yet. I've heard they can be quite expensive. But at the same time, I've been noticing a lot of people around me talking about being more eco-friendly.
Assistant: That's a great point. Many people are becoming more aware of their environmental impact, and EVs are one way to reduce your carbon footprint. The prices of EVs are also decreasing as technology improves.
User: I see. It sounds like a good option. But what's driving this sudden interest in being more environmentally friendly?
Assistant: I think it's a combination of factors, including increased awareness about climate change and its effects. People are starting to realize that their daily choices, such as the cars they drive, can have a significant impact on the environment.
User: That makes sense. I've been noticing a shift in values among my friends and family, especially when it comes to transportation.
Assistant: Yes, the way people think about transportation is changing. Gas-guzzling cars are no longer seen as the status symbol they once were. Instead, people are opting for more sustainable options.
User: Exactly! Environmental concerns and a growing awareness of the carbon footprint of gas-guzzling cars have led to a shift in values. I'm starting to think that my old SUV might not be the best choice anymore.
Assistant: It sounds like you're part of this shift in values. If you're willing to make a change, there are many great alternatives available. Would you like me to suggest some eco-friendly car models that might suit your needs?
User: That would be great, thank you. I'd love to explore some options that align with my new values.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help. Let me provide you with some information on electric and hybrid vehicles that are currently on the market.
User: Sounds good. I'm looking forward to learning more about these sustainable options.
Assistant: I'll provide you with a list of models, their features, and benefits. This will help you make an informed decision when choosing your next car.

User: Hey, I'm looking for a new hobby to get into on the weekends. Do you have any ideas?
Assistant: There are so many great options out there. What are your interests? Are you more of a thrill-seeker or do you prefer something relaxing?
User: Hmm, I think I'm a mix of both. I like to unwind, but I also enjoy activities that get my adrenaline pumping.
Assistant: That's a great combination. Some ideas that come to mind are extreme sports, like rock climbing or skydiving, but if you're looking for something a bit more low-key, you could try hiking or kayaking.
User: Those sound like good options, but I'm not sure if I'm ready to commit to something that intense. Do you have any other suggestions?
Assistant: Well, what about cars? Are you into cars at all?
User: Actually, yes! I've always been a car enthusiast. I love the way they look, the way they sound... everything.
Assistant: Ah, a petrolhead! In that case, have you ever considered taking your car to a racing track?
User: (pauses) You know, I think I've always wanted to do that, but I never thought it was possible. I mean, isn't it just for professional drivers?

User: Hey, I've been thinking about buying a new car, but I'm not sure where to start. There are so many models out there, and I don't know what features I should be looking for.
Assistant: Buying a new car can be overwhelming, but it's exciting at the same time. What's your current ride like, and what are you looking for in a new car? More space, better fuel efficiency, or maybe something with more style?
User: Yeah, I've had my current car for years, and it's been reliable, but I think it's time for an upgrade. I'm looking for something with more advanced safety features and better fuel efficiency. I've heard a lot about electric cars, but I'm not sure if they're worth the investment.
Assistant: Electric cars are definitely worth considering, especially with the rising fuel costs and environmental concerns. They've come a long way in terms of performance and range, but it ultimately depends on your lifestyle and driving habits. Do you have a daily commute, or do you drive mostly on weekends?
User: I drive to work every day, about 30 miles each way, so I'd need something that can handle that. But I also like to take road trips on the weekends, so range is important to me.
Assistant: Okay, that helps narrow it down. There are many electric cars that can handle your daily commute and weekend road trips. Have you considered the Tesla Model 3 or the Hyundai Kona Electric? They both have great range and are relatively affordable.
User: Actually, I've been watching some YouTube reviews of those models, and they seem like great options. But I'm also interested in the new Honda Civic Hybrid. I've heard it's a great compromise between fuel efficiency and performance.
Assistant: Ah, the Honda Civic Hybrid is a great choice too! It's a more affordable option than some of the electric cars, and it still offers great fuel efficiency. The YouTube reviews are a great way to get a feel for the car's features and performance. Which reviewers do you usually watch?
User: I often spend my free time watching car reviews and comparisons on YouTube to stay up-to-date on the latest models and trends. I love watching Doug DeMuro's in-depth reviews and Chris Harris's test drives. They give me a great sense of what each car is like to drive and own.
Assistant: Those guys are great! Doug DeMuro's attention to detail is impressive, and Chris Harris's enthusiasm is infectious. If you're watching their reviews, you're probably getting a good sense of the pros and cons of each car. What do you think is the most important factor in your decision-making process?
User: For me, it's a combination of factors – safety features, fuel efficiency, performance, and price. I want a car that checks all those boxes and still looks great on the road.
Assistant: That's a great approach. Now that we've narrowed down your options, I'd recommend making a spreadsheet to compare the features and prices of each car. Sometimes, seeing everything side-by-side can help make the decision clearer. Would you like me to help you set up a spreadsheet?
User: Yeah, that would be really helpful. I'm not the most spreadsheet-savvy person, so a little guidance would be great.
Assistant: No problem! I can walk you through it. We can start by listing the cars you're interested in and their respective features, prices, and pros and cons. Then, we can use formulas to compare the data and see which car comes out on top. Sound good?
User: Hey, I just got back from a week-long trip and I'm still feeling pretty refreshed. I think I've figured out the secret to a perfect vacation.
Assistant: That sounds amazing! I'm glad to hear you're feeling refreshed. What do you think is the key to a perfect vacation? Is it the destination, the activities, or something else entirely?
User: For me, it's all about finding the right balance between relaxation and excitement. I don't want to just sit around doing nothing, but at the same time, I don't want to be too stressed out about trying to cram in a million activities.
Assistant: That makes sense. It's all about finding that sweet spot. So, what kind of activities do you usually enjoy doing on vacation? Are you more of an outdoorsy person or do you prefer exploring cities?
User: I'm definitely a fan of the outdoors. I love hiking, camping, and just exploring nature in general. But I also enjoy driving and taking in the scenery from the road.
Assistant: There's something special about taking a drive through a beautiful landscape, isn't there? The freedom of the open road, the wind in your hair... it's a great way to clear your head and enjoy the views. Do you have a favorite road trip route or a dream drive that you've always wanted to take?
User: Actually, I do. I've always wanted to drive along the coast, with the ocean on one side and the cliffs on the other. It sounds like the perfect combination of natural beauty and thrilling driving.
Assistant: That sounds incredible! There's something about the ocean that's just so captivating. And when you add in the thrill of driving a winding coastal road, it's like the ultimate driving experience. What kind of car would you want to take on a drive like that?
User: Ah, that's an easy one – my favorite sports car, of course! There's something about the way it hugs the road and responds to every turn that just makes me feel alive.
Assistant: I can imagine! Taking a scenic drive along a winding coastal road in a sports car is basically the ultimate driving experience. The speed, the agility, the stunning views... it's like a match made in heaven. Have you ever actually done a drive like that before, or is it still on your bucket list?
User: Actually, I have done it before, and it's truly the perfect way for me to unwind and enjoy the thrill of driving. Taking a scenic drive along a winding coastal road in my favorite sports car is the perfect way for me to clear my head and just enjoy the moment.
Assistant: That sounds amazing. I can see why it's your go-to way to unwind. There's something about the combination of natural beauty, thrilling driving, and the freedom of the open road that's just so captivating. Do you have a favorite part of the drive, or is it more about the overall experience for you?
User: For me, it's definitely about the overall experience. I love the way the road winds and twists, the way the light reflects off the ocean, and the sound of the waves crashing against the shore. It's just so immersive and engaging.
Assistant: I can imagine! It sounds like you're completely in the moment when you're driving, which is great. Being present and mindful can be really beneficial for both your mental and physical health. Do you find that driving has any other benefits for you, or is it mainly just a way to unwind and have fun?
User: Actually, I think driving has a lot of benefits for me. It helps me clear my head, work through problems, and just gain a new perspective on things. Plus, it's a great way to challenge myself and push my limits, which is always a thrill.
Assistant: That's really interesting. I think a lot of people underestimate the benefits of driving and just see it as a way to get from point A to point B. But for you, it's clearly so much more than that. Do you think you'll be taking any more scenic drives in the near future, or are you already planning your next adventure?

c101-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Here is a piece of text: ‘You look like you’ve seen a ghost,” observes a neighbour. SEEN a ghost? I’ve just driven one — a Rolls-Royce Ghost EWB — and while it doesn’t leave me pale with fright, it does bring on a certain shade of green. Envy, I think.
My wife, Pat, and I were celebrating our 50th anniversary, a milestone statistics say only five per cent of married couples reach. That means a couple of five percenters got to live like one percenters, if only for a couple of days.
When Patrick Kirkwood of Ferrari Maserati Roll Royce of Alberta handed me the key to the most luxurious automobile I’ve driven in 20 plus years of reviewing cars, it had a mere eight kilometres on the odometer.
First impressions? This car carries its bulk — 2,970 kilograms — with dignity and style. Proportions are spot on and the subtle two-tone paintwork is flawless.
I love the “suicide” rear doors which allow a wide area for a rather majestic entry or exit should one desire to make that impression. Front passengers enjoy 1,060 mm (41.7 in.) of legroom while rear riders can stretch out across 1,245 mm (49 in.) of space. And there’s lots of room to carry luggage for all occasions in the 490L trunk (oops, I mean boot).
The interior is pure luxury: leather, wood, even deep lamb’s wool floor mats that encouraged Pat to kick off her shoes and wriggle her toes in that deep, soft, pile as she leaned back in her seat to enjoy the ride.
Her chauffeur (me) kept his shoes on.
It was cloudy when we left, but the panoramic sunroof kept the interior bright. Passengers get a fold-down centre console to allow control of telephone, the bespoke audio’s functions, a map display and seat adjustments. Add in creature features like rear theatre and picnic tables and it seemed a shame we didn’t have a chauffeur…except I like to drive and this car is a dream to pilot down the highway.
While there’s an abundance of electronics on board the Ghost, it’s the simplicity of the features that’s striking. Controls are easy to use, thoughtfully laid out and they don’t cause distraction for the driver. It took very little time to become completely at home with the location and operation of controls and switches. No annoyingly complicated dance through non-intuitive menus here. Within 15 minutes I was comfortable with all the systems. It seems even sensible controls are a luxury these days.
A host of driver assistance programs were on tap including active cruise control with stop and go, lane departure warning, head-up display, side view camera, rear-view camera with top view and all the usual driving nannies. The optional night vision camera provided a ghostly image of animals and humans within its considerable coverage range.
Our anniversary route took us from Calgary to the Post Hotel in Lake Louise, a luxury establishment famous for its service, attention to detail, great wine cellar and outstanding kitchen. Hey, you gotta splurge on your 50th anniversary!
In a car like this, you never take the direct route. Getting there is way more than half the fun, besides the Trans Canada is a bit boring and I wanted to experience the Ghost more fully.
For such a big vehicle, it’s surprisingly nimble and all that subdued elegance hides a playful side. There’s more than enough muscle to move it along with a satisfying surge of acceleration. Power from the 563 horsepower of its 6.5L V-12 engine gets to the rear wheels through a near-seamless eight-speed automatic transmission. Pushed by 605 pound-feet of torque, the combination propels the Ghost to 100 km/h in five seconds and passing velocities on the highway are attained in spook-tacular fashion.
Ghost is by no means a fuel-sipper even when driven sedately, but then if you own or lease one of these beauties, the 15.3 L/100 km I averaged poses no financial burden when re-filling the 82.5L tank with premium gasoline.
A host of optional equipment boosted the $337,275 entry price to a total of $473,443.95 (including fees, $5,800 for freight and $3,800 for PDI). Of course GST is extra bringing the tab to just under a half-million bucks.
There’s not a ghost of a chance I will afford one of these beauties with the Spirit of Ecstasy on the hood, but it was nice to act the part for a few days.
Harry Pegg is a member of the Automobile Journalists Association of Canada.
Harry and Pat in the summer of 1966. They are still motoring together 50 years later.

User: Here is a piece of text: ‘You look like you’ve seen a ghost,” observes a neighbour. SEEN a ghost? I’ve just driven one — a Rolls-Royce Ghost EWB — and while it doesn’t leave me pale with fright, it does bring on a certain shade of green. Envy, I think.
My wife, Pat, and I were celebrating our 50th anniversary, a milestone statistics say only five per cent of married couples reach. That means a couple of five percenters got to live like one percenters, if only for a couple of days.
When Patrick Kirkwood of Ferrari Maserati Roll Royce of Alberta handed me the key to the most luxurious automobile I’ve driven in 20 plus years of reviewing cars, it had a mere eight kilometres on the odometer.
First impressions? This car carries its bulk — 2,970 kilograms — with dignity and style. Proportions are spot on and the subtle two-tone paintwork is flawless.
I love the “suicide” rear doors which allow a wide area for a rather majestic entry or exit should one desire to make that impression. Front passengers enjoy 1,060 mm (41.7 in.) of legroom while rear riders can stretch out across 1,245 mm (49 in.) of space. And there’s lots of room to carry luggage for all occasions in the 490L trunk (oops, I mean boot).
The interior is pure luxury: leather, wood, even deep lamb’s wool floor mats that encouraged Pat to kick off her shoes and wriggle her toes in that deep, soft, pile as she leaned back in her seat to enjoy the ride.
Her chauffeur (me) kept his shoes on.
It was cloudy when we left, but the panoramic sunroof kept the interior bright. Passengers get a fold-down centre console to allow control of telephone, the bespoke audio’s functions, a map display and seat adjustments. Add in creature features like rear theatre and picnic tables and it seemed a shame we didn’t have a chauffeur…except I like to drive and this car is a dream to pilot down the highway.
While there’s an abundance of electronics on board the Ghost, it’s the simplicity of the features that’s striking. Controls are easy to use, thoughtfully laid out and they don’t cause distraction for the driver. It took very little time to become completely at home with the location and operation of controls and switches. No annoyingly complicated dance through non-intuitive menus here. Within 15 minutes I was comfortable with all the systems. It seems even sensible controls are a luxury these days.
A host of driver assistance programs were on tap including active cruise control with stop and go, lane departure warning, head-up display, side view camera, rear-view camera with top view and all the usual driving nannies. The optional night vision camera provided a ghostly image of animals and humans within its considerable coverage range.
Our anniversary route took us from Calgary to the Post Hotel in Lake Louise, a luxury establishment famous for its service, attention to detail, great wine cellar and outstanding kitchen. Hey, you gotta splurge on your 50th anniversary!
In a car like this, you never take the direct route. Getting there is way more than half the fun, besides the Trans Canada is a bit boring and I wanted to experience the Ghost more fully.
For such a big vehicle, it’s surprisingly nimble and all that subdued elegance hides a playful side. There’s more than enough muscle to move it along with a satisfying surge of acceleration. Power from the 563 horsepower of its 6.5L V-12 engine gets to the rear wheels through a near-seamless eight-speed automatic transmission. Pushed by 605 pound-feet of torque, the combination propels the Ghost to 100 km/h in five seconds and passing velocities on the highway are attained in spook-tacular fashion.
Ghost is by no means a fuel-sipper even when driven sedately, but then if you own or lease one of these beauties, the 15.3 L/100 km I averaged poses no financial burden when re-filling the 82.5L tank with premium gasoline.
A host of optional equipment boosted the $337,275 entry price to a total of $473,443.95 (including fees, $5,800 for freight and $3,800 for PDI). Of course GST is extra bringing the tab to just under a half-million bucks.
There’s not a ghost of a chance I will afford one of these beauties with the Spirit of Ecstasy on the hood, but it was nice to act the part for a few days.
Harry Pegg is a member of the Automobile Journalists Association of Canada.
Harry and Pat in the summer of 1966. They are still motoring together 50 years later.

I love the “suicide” rear doors which allow a wide area for a rather majestic entry or exit should one desire to make that impression. Front passengers enjoy 1,060 mm (41.7 in.) of legroom while rear riders can stretch out across 1,245 mm (49 in.) of space. And there’s lots of room to carry luggage for all occasions in the 490L trunk (oops, I mean boot).
The interior is pure luxury: leather, wood, even deep lamb’s wool floor mats that encouraged Pat to kick off her shoes and wriggle her toes in that deep, soft, pile as she leaned back in her seat to enjoy the ride.
Her chauffeur (me) kept his shoes on.
It was cloudy when we left, but the panoramic sunroof kept the interior bright. Passengers get a fold-down centre console to allow control of telephone, the bespoke audio’s functions, a map display and seat adjustments. Add in creature features like rear theatre and picnic tables and it seemed a shame we didn’t have a chauffeur…except I like to drive and this car is a dream to pilot down the highway.
While there’s an abundance of electronics on board the Ghost, it’s the simplicity of the features that’s striking. Controls are easy to use, thoughtfully laid out and they don’t cause distraction for the driver. It took very little time to become completely at home with the location and operation of controls and switches. No annoyingly complicated dance through non-intuitive menus here. Within 15 minutes I was comfortable with all the systems. It seems even sensible controls are a luxury these days.
A host of driver assistance programs were on tap including active cruise control with stop and go, lane departure warning, head-up display, side view camera, rear-view camera with top view and all the usual driving nannies. The optional night vision camera provided a ghostly image of animals and humans within its considerable coverage range.
Our anniversary route took us from Calgary to the Post Hotel in Lake Louise, a luxury establishment famous for its service, attention to detail, great wine cellar and outstanding kitchen. Hey, you gotta splurge on your 50th anniversary!
In a car like this, you never take the direct route. Getting there is way more than half the fun, besides the Trans Canada is a bit boring and I wanted to experience the Ghost more fully.
For such a big vehicle, it’s surprisingly nimble and all that subdued elegance hides a playful side. There’s more than enough muscle to move it along with a satisfying surge of acceleration. Power from the 563 horsepower of its 6.5L V-12 engine gets to the rear wheels through a near-seamless eight-speed automatic transmission. Pushed by 605 pound-feet of torque, the combination propels the Ghost to 100 km/h in five seconds and passing velocities on the highway are attained in spook-tacular fashion.
Ghost is by no means a fuel-sipper even when driven sedately, but then if you own or lease one of these beauties, the 15.3 L/100 km I averaged poses no financial burden when re-filling the 82.5L tank with premium gasoline.
A host of optional equipment boosted the $337,275 entry price to a total of $473,443.95 (including fees, $5,800 for freight and $3,800 for PDI). Of course GST is extra bringing the tab to just under a half-million bucks.
There’s not a ghost of a chance I will afford one of these beauties with the Spirit of Ecstasy on the hood, but it was nice to act the part for a few days.

Harry and Pat in the summer of 1966. They are still motoring together 50 years later.

User: Here is a piece of text: Time was, Chevy Camaros looked good and went fast in a straight line, but that was about it. Then the ‘90s came along and Camaros couldn’t even do that, unless you paid for the SS.
In 2014 the Camaro has become an entirely different beast. The track tuned Z28 just managed a lap of the Nurburgring in 7:37.40, faster than a Porsche 911 Carrera S or a Lexus LFA.
For those of you who don’t know, the Nurburgring track has corners…lots of them. Traditionally, corners have been the arch nemesis of American performance cars. So how did this hulking beast with a 7.0-liter V8 just do beat a precision Japanese supercar like the LFA?
For starters, the suspension has been completely revised, allowing the car to handle 1.08 g of acceleration through the corners. The Brembo brakes are much bigger than the ones fitted to the standard car. And the big brakes are made from carbon, as opposed to the particularly dense cheese that seems to be used on old Camaros.
In a truly un-American fashion, Chevy designers stripped out all unnecessary weight from the Z28.
Put this together with a thundering 505 horsepower, race-derived V8 and the results are heart stopping.
Watching the in-car footage, which you can see below, is staggering. The Z28 hammers around slow corners at 60-70 mph and hits 160 on the straights. The soundtrack is just as mesmerizing. The massive aluminum block V8 roars from baritone to tenor as the driver slams through gears on the short throw six-speed. It’s a wonderful combination of pony car thrum and Indy car scream.
As good as the car is – and looks – the performance of test driver Adam Dean may just be better. The lap starts in the clear, albeit with a damp track surface, but by the time the car hits the back straight the driver is battling rain at speeds of 150 mph.
Given the rear-wheel drive Z28’s propensity to step out in the corners – as we see in several sphincter tightening moments – that feat took courage and balls of steel – and probably ovaries, too. Chevy engineers claim that their telemetry indicates the lap would have been a full six seconds faster on a dry track. Hopefully we get to see that.
Maybe just as impressive as the lap, though less captivating, was the testing this car was put through while at the dreaded ‘Ring. Chevy put its Camaro through 1,000 miles of laps, none which could have more than a two-percent variance from the target lap time in a 24 hour period. That, dear reader, is insane.
No word on price yet. We can hope and dream, though, that it won’t be as out of reach as the supercars the Camaro Z28 dethroned on the Nurburgring Nordschleife.

Question/Instruction: Continue the author's list of things he misses from the past, adding your own personal experiences and memories.

Given material: Some of you, most of all of you over 50, remember when the new cars used to come out with great fanfare. My recollection is that it was about this time of year, perhaps a few weeks sooner. In Perry, Cecil Moody had Fords, my grandfather, Charles Gray, had Chevys and Calvin McClendon had Dodges and Plymouths. All of these dealerships were in downtown Perry. Three good dealerships, three good men.
Unlike today, all of the cars looked considerably different from year to year. Think: a 1957 Chevy, a 1958 Chevy and a 1959 Chevy. You could tell when you saw one what make it was and what year it was. Today, I can’t tell the difference in Ford, Chevy and Honda SUVs, when I meet them on the road. When the new cars used to come out, it was almost as big as the fair coming. I miss the old-time new car shows.
Folks in Perry, well, at least the men, used to have gathering places where they met, drank coffee and solved the country’s problems. When I was “coming along,” the group I attended met at the Coffee Cup in downtown Perry. There were three morning shifts, one about 6:30, one at 7:30 and one about 8:30 with some “bleeding over” from one to the other. Lots of banter, lots of bull and lots of opinions. But, you’ve got to admit that things worked better back then than now. Maybe if we had these places today, politically things would be better. I miss these gatherings.
I don’t have a place to go and hang out, a few minutes, maybe 30 or less, when I tire of the law office and just want to get out for a little while. I used to go to the feed and seed store, Walker and Thompson, and visit with Mr. Ed, Mr. Glea, Mrs. Middlebrooks and Joe Hodges. Or, I could go uptown to the Swank Shop and visit and listen to Billy Bledsoe. Or, I could drop by Union Motor Company and talk with Uncle Norman and Uncle Thomas or go down to Walker-Rhodes Tractor and visit Daddy and Foster. I miss a place to just go and hang out for a little while.
Truth of the matter, I miss the South and how it used to be. I miss Perry and how it was. I miss the way Southerners used to talk — the way they sounded. I miss donkey basketball, Tom Thumb weddings, womanless weddings, dances at the National Guard Armory, Perry High School basketball, the arcade, dance hall and the bowling alley at Houston Lake, feed stores, seed stores, baby chicks (biddies) for sale, hog feed, cotton gins, turnip seeds, drink boxes with ice cold water and grape drinks in bottles, merchants that would let you charge and would cash your check, and fishing for bream on the bed. And then, there were those three drugstores in downtown Perry with all three having soda fountains.
These are some of the things I miss. And, there’s lots more, but I guess I’ll just have to get over it and move on. That’s what I’ve done so far.

In Perry, Cecil Moody had Fords, my grandfather, Charles Gray, had Chevys and Calvin McClendon had Dodges and Plymouths. All of these dealerships were in downtown Perry. Three good dealerships, three good men.
Unlike today, all of the cars looked considerably different from year to year. Think: a 1957 Chevy, a 1958 Chevy and a 1959 Chevy. You could tell when you saw one what make it was and what year it was. Today, I can’t tell the difference in Ford, Chevy and Honda SUVs, when I meet them on the road. When the new cars used to come out, it was almost as big as the fair coming. I miss the old-time new car shows.
Folks in Perry, well, at least the men, used to have gathering places where they met, drank coffee and solved the country’s problems. When I was “coming along,” the group I attended met at the Coffee Cup in downtown Perry. There were three morning shifts, one about 6:30, one at 7:30 and one about 8:30 with some “bleeding over” from one to the other. Lots of banter, lots of bull and lots of opinions. But, you’ve got to admit that things worked better back then than now. Maybe if we had these places today, politically things would be better. I miss these gatherings.
I don’t have a place to go and hang out, a few minutes, maybe 30 or less, when I tire of the law office and just want to get out for a little while. I used to go to the feed and seed store, Walker and Thompson, and visit with Mr. Ed, Mr. Glea, Mrs. Middlebrooks and Joe Hodges. Or, I could go uptown to the Swank Shop and visit and listen to Billy Bledsoe. Or, I could drop by Union Motor Company and talk with Uncle Norman and Uncle Thomas or go down to Walker-Rhodes Tractor and visit Daddy and Foster. I miss a place to just go and hang out for a little while.
Truth of the matter, I miss the South and how it used to be. I miss Perry and how it was. I miss the way Southerners used to talk — the way they sounded. I miss donkey basketball, Tom Thumb weddings, womanless weddings, dances at the National Guard Armory, Perry High School basketball, the arcade, dance hall and the bowling alley at Houston Lake, feed stores, seed stores, baby chicks (biddies) for sale, hog feed, cotton gins, turnip seeds, drink boxes with ice cold water and grape drinks in bottles, merchants that would let you charge and would cash your check, and fishing for bream on the bed. And then, there were those three drugstores in downtown Perry with all three having soda fountains.
These are some of the things I miss. And, there’s lots more, but I guess I’ll just have to get over it and move on. That’s what I’ve done so far.
